3	Hybrid linear recurrent architectures---including GatedDeltaNet (GDN), RetNet, HGRN2, Gated Linear Attention (GLA), and DeltaNet---achieve aggregate benchmark scores within 1--2 points of each other at matched parameter budgets. Yet they can differ on up to 90\% of the individual examples they affect: adding attention to three controlled linear recurrent backbones yields helped and hurt sets with at most 10\% pairwise overlap, approximately twice the independence baseline. This per-example divergence is invisible in aggregate metrics: architectures that score within 1--2 points of each other reach similar accuracy by gaining and losing on different inputs. Across all ten pairwise comparisons among five architectures, overlap in per-example effects remains below 14\% (all $p < .01$), meaning the choice of backbone is associated with which specific inputs a deployed system handles correctly.

tool_args.old_string: These studies attribute divergence to initialization noise or the near-optimal set within a single architecture. Rashomon-set analyses \citep{fisher2019all,semenova2022existence,jain2025allocation} examine variation among near-optimal models within a single hypothesis class; ensemble diversity work \citep{fort2019deep,kuncheva2003measures,brown2005diversity} shows that diverse architectures explore distinct loss-landscape modes. Weight-space interpolation \citep{wortsman2022model} can reduce multiplicity among models of a single architecture; we instead characterize multiplicity across architectures, where interpolation is not applicable. Our routing approach relates to selective prediction \citep{geifman2017selective} and ensemble selection \citep{caruana2004ensemble}, though we select among architecturally distinct models rather than same-architecture ensembles. We show that changing the recurrent backbone---without explicit diversification---is associated with per-example multiplicity that varies systematically by task type. \citet{swayamdipta2020dataset} characterize examples via training dynamics; our decomposition operates at deployment time across architectures. Our cross-benchmark variation ($\alpha = 0.14$--$0.30$) argues against single-artifact explanations \citep{niven2019probing}. The observation that aggregate associations can diverge from individual-level patterns is a well-known statistical phenomenon (ecological fallacy; \citealt{robinson1950ecological}); our finding (\S\ref{ssec:decoupling}) is a controlled instance within recurrent architectural families. \citet{yang2026benchmark} demonstrate this phenomenon at the frontier-LLM level, showing 16--66\% per-item disagreement despite comparable benchmark accuracy; our work provides a controlled within-family analysis that isolates backbone variation from training-regime differences.
tool_args.new_string: These studies attribute divergence to initialization noise or the near-optimal set within a single architecture. Our routing approach relates to selective prediction \citep{geifman2017selective} and ensemble selection \citep{caruana2004ensemble}, though we select among architecturally distinct models rather than same-architecture ensembles. We show that changing the recurrent backbone is associated with per-example multiplicity that varies by task type; \citet{swayamdipta2020dataset} characterize examples via training dynamics, while our decomposition operates at deployment time. \citet{yang2026benchmark} demonstrate analogous per-item disagreement (16--66\%) among frontier LLMs; our within-family design isolates backbone variation from training-regime differences.

tool_args.new_string: An alternative interpretation of the saturation is that adding even minimal attention causes all architectures to rapidly adopt Transformer-like behavior, rather than locking in architecture-specific fingerprints. Appendix~\ref{app:transformer_entrainment} shows that h3-1 correct sets indeed converge toward the Transformer baseline, consistent with this account. Under the fingerprint view, each recurrent backbone imposes a characteristic inductive bias that determines which examples attention can rescue; under the convergence view, attention overrides backbone differences and steers all architectures toward a shared solution, with residual per-example divergence arising from incomplete convergence. Disentangling these accounts requires ablation of the attention mechanism itself---for example, replacing learned attention weights with random projections---which we leave to future work.
